Chapter 18 — Parabola

Kanna, a parabola is a distance rule. Understand the focus and directrix first; the equation then has a picture.

Your overall target remains 200 marks: Physics 60, Maths 60, Chemistry 80. Standard forms, shifts, a point parameter, tangent recognition and simple distance/area models are useful first steps. The supplied normal-count example comes later; it does not require learning the general cubic formula.

Important for JEE Main: the official coordinate-geometry unit explicitly includes standard conic equations, including parabola. The core below explains those equations and their geometry. Tangent, normal, focal-chord, subnormal and other constructions are retained as supporting tools for this supplied PDF; each is not claimed as a separately named official syllabus topic. Priorities here are teaching judgments, not measured formula-frequency ranks.

Concept C01 — Equal distance from a point and a line

Fix a point FFF, called the focus, and a line ddd, called the directrix. The focus is not on that line. A parabola consists of all points PPP satisfying

PF=perpendicular distance from P to the directrix.\boxed{PF=\text{perpendicular distance from }P\text{ to the directrix}}.PF=perpendicular distance from P to the directrix​.

The distance to a line always means the shortest, perpendicular segment. It is not a sloping segment chosen at will.

The axis is the line through the focus perpendicular to the directrix. The vertex is where the curve meets that axis. It lies halfway between the focus and the nearest point on the directrix.

For focus (a,0)(a,0)(a,0) and directrix x=−ax=-ax=−a, with a>0a>0a>0, write P=(x,y)P=(x,y)P=(x,y). Equal distances give

(x−a)2+y2=∣x+a∣.\sqrt{(x-a)^2+y^2}=|x+a|.(x−a)2+y2​=∣x+a∣.

Both sides are nonnegative, so squaring is safe:

(x−a)2+y2=(x+a)2⟹y2=4ax.(x-a)^2+y^2=(x+a)^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{y^2=4ax}.(x−a)2+y2=(x+a)2⟹y2=4ax​.

This equation forces x≥0x\ge0x≥0, so the parabola opens right. Its vertex is (0,0)(0,0)(0,0) and axis is y=0y=0y=0.

The distance ratio e=PF/PDe=PF/PDe=PF/PD is called eccentricity, where DDD is the directrix foot. A parabola has e=1e=1e=1. It has no centre like a circle; its focus and vertex are different points.

Pattern: the unsquared variable tells the opening direction; its sign chooses positive or negative. A squared yyy means a horizontal axis. A squared xxx means a vertical axis.

Complete squares before reading a shifted parabola. For example, x2+6x−12y+33=0x^2+6x-12y+33=0x2+6x−12y+33=0 becomes (x+3)2=12(y−2)(x+3)^2=12(y-2)(x+3)2=12(y−2): vertex (−3,2)(-3,2)(−3,2), opening up.

For a quadratic graph y=Ax2+Bx+Cy=Ax^2+Bx+Cy=Ax2+Bx+C, A≠0A\ne0A=0:

h=−B2A,k=C−B24A,y−k=A(x−h)2.h=-\frac{B}{2A},\qquad k=C-\frac{B^2}{4A},\qquad y-k=A(x-h)^2.h=−2AB​,k=C−4AB2​,y−k=A(x−h)2.

Its signed focal parameter is p=1/(4A)p=1/(4A)p=1/(4A). Thus focus (h,k+p)(h,k+p)(h,k+p), directrix y=k−py=k-py=k−p, and positive focal length ∣p∣|p|∣p∣. Positive AAA opens up; negative AAA opens down.

Important for JEE Main: the coefficient AAA is not the focal length. A larger positive AAA makes the parabola narrower and its focus closer to the vertex. Q29 uses A=2A=2A=2 but focal length 1/81/81/8.

Concept C03 — Focal distance and the latus rectum

For y2=4axy^2=4axy2=4ax with a>0a>0a>0, the definition gives the focal distance

PF=x+a.\boxed{PF=x+a}.PF=x+a​.

It is already a length, not a squared length. It is at least aaa, with equality at the vertex.

A chord joins two different curve points. A focal chord is a chord whose line passes through the focus. The latus rectum is the focal chord perpendicular to the axis.

For y2=4axy^2=4axy2=4ax, its line is x=ax=ax=a. Substitute:

y2=4a2⟹A=(a,2a),B=(a,−2a).y^2=4a^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad A=(a,2a),\quad B=(a,-2a).y2=4a2⟹A=(a,2a),B=(a,−2a).

Therefore

latus-rectum length=4a.\boxed{\text{latus-rectum length}=4a}.latus-rectum length=4a​.

The vertex–latus-endpoints triangle has base 4a4a4a, perpendicular height aaa, and area 2a22a^22a2. For other orientations, rotate or shift the same geometry; the length is still 4a4a4a.

Exception to notice: the axis itself passes through the focus but meets the parabola only at its vertex. It does not create a finite two-endpoint focal chord. Q7 tests this.

For translated right-opening (y−k)2=4a(x−h)(y-k)^2=4a(x-h)(y−k)2=4a(x−h), the focal distance is x−h+ax-h+ax−h+a. For the other openings, use the distance to their stated directrix; do not copy x+ax+ax+a to an upward or left-opening parabola.

Concept C04 — A parameter labels a point and simplifies a chord

For y2=4axy^2=4axy2=4ax, every point is

P(t)=(at2,2at),t∈R.\boxed{P(t)=(at^2,2at)},\qquad t\in\mathbb R.P(t)=(at2,2at)​,t∈R.

Substitution checks it: (2at)2=4a(at2)(2at)^2=4a(at^2)(2at)2=4a(at2). Positive ttt gives the upper half, negative ttt the lower half, and t=0t=0t=0 the vertex. A parameter is a number used to label a point; ttt is not automatically an angle.

For two distinct parameters t1,t2t_1,t_2t1​,t2​, the chord is

(t1+t2)y=2x+2at1t2.\boxed{(t_1+t_2)y=2x+2at_1t_2}.(t1​+t2​)y=2x+2at1​t2​​.

Check it at P(t1)P(t_1)P(t1​): the left side is 2at1(t1+t2)2at_1(t_1+t_2)2at1​(t1​+t2​); the right side is 2at12+2at1t22at_1^2+2at_1t_22at12​+2at1​t2​, the same. The second endpoint works too.

If t1+t2=0t_1+t_2=0t1​+t2​=0, the chord is vertical. The equation still works without dividing. Otherwise its slope is 2/(t1+t2)2/(t_1+t_2)2/(t1​+t2​).

For the upward form x2=4ayx^2=4ayx2=4ay, swap the roles: P(t)=(2at,at2)P(t)=(2at,at^2)P(t)=(2at,at2). For shifts, add the vertex coordinates after constructing the corresponding standard point.

Concept C05 — Tangent: same direction at the touching point

A tangent gives the curve's local direction. At a nonvertex point (x1,y1)(x_1,y_1)(x1​,y1​) of y2=4axy^2=4axy2=4ax,

2yy′=4a⟹y′=2ay.2yy'=4a\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y'=\frac{2a}{y}.2yy′=4a⟹y′=y2a​.

Using point-slope form and y12=4ax1y_1^2=4ax_1y12​=4ax1​ gives

yy1=2a(x+x1).\boxed{yy_1=2a(x+x_1)}.yy1​=2a(x+x1​)​.

At P(t)P(t)P(t) this becomes

ty=x+at2.\boxed{ty=x+at^2}.ty=x+at2​.

The parameter form includes t=0t=0t=0, giving the vertical vertex tangent x=0x=0x=0. The derivative formula with division by yyy must handle the vertex separately.

For a finite slope m≠0m\ne0m=0, t=1/mt=1/mt=1/m gives

y=mx+am.\boxed{y=mx+\frac am}.y=mx+ma​​.

There is no finite horizontal tangent to the right-opening parabola. Its vertex tangent is vertical. For a general proper line Ax+By+C=0Ax+By+C=0Ax+By+C=0, substitution into the parabola yields the tangency condition

AC=aB2.\boxed{AC=aB^2}.AC=aB2​.

To see why when A≠0A\ne0A=0, substitute x=−(By+C)/Ax=-(By+C)/Ax=−(By+C)/A:

Ay2+4aBy+4aC=0.Ay^2+4aBy+4aC=0.Ay2+4aBy+4aC=0.

Its repeated-root condition is 16a2B2−16aAC=016a^2B^2-16aAC=016a2B2−16aAC=0. The same condition includes x=0x=0x=0 and excludes horizontal lines.

A trap specific to parabolas: a line parallel to the axis can meet the curve at one finite point without being tangent. For example, y=1y=1y=1 cuts y2=4axy^2=4axy2=4ax once, but its slope is 0 while the curve's slope there is 2a2a2a. “Only one intersection” alone is not a safe tangent definition for an unbounded curve.

Tangents from (x0,y0)(x_0,y_0)(x0​,y0​): put the point in the parameter tangent:

at2−y0t+x0=0.\boxed{at^2-y_0t+x_0=0}.at2−y0​t+x0​=0​.

Every real root labels a contact point and a tangent, including a possible vertex tangent. Its discriminant is

D=y02−4ax0.\boxed{D=y_0^2-4ax_0}.D=y02​−4ax0​​.

D>0D>0D>0 gives two distinct tangents, D=0D=0D=0 one, D<0D<0D<0 none. This is a safe count because the leading coefficient aaa is nonzero.

When using finite slopes instead, the equation is x0m2−y0m+a=0x_0m^2-y_0m+a=0x0​m2−y0​m+a=0. It can become linear at x0=0x_0=0x0​=0, so check the vertical member separately.

For a point on the directrix x0=−ax_0=-ax0​=−a, the two finite tangent slopes have product a/x0=−1a/x_0=-1a/x0​=−1. Thus the tangents are perpendicular. Q14 derives this in its actual data.

Concept C06 — Focal chords connect opposite-sign parameters

Put focus F=(a,0)F=(a,0)F=(a,0) into the chord equation from C04:

0=2a+2at1t2⟹t1t2=−1.0=2a+2at_1t_2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{t_1t_2=-1}.0=2a+2at1​t2​⟹t1​t2​=−1​.

So if one endpoint has t≠0t\ne0t=0, the other has −1/t-1/t−1/t. Their ordinates have opposite signs, and the focus lies between the endpoints.

The focal distances of its two ends are

s1=a(1+t2),s2=a(1+t−2).s_1=a(1+t^2),\qquad s_2=a(1+t^{-2}).s1​=a(1+t2),s2​=a(1+t−2).

Add them to get the chord length:

L=a(t+1t)2.\boxed{L=a\left(t+\frac1t\right)^2}.L=a(t+t1​)2​.

Related useful identities are

1s1+1s2=1a,s1s2=aL.\boxed{\frac1{s_1}+\frac1{s_2}=\frac1a},\qquad s_1s_2=aL.s1​1​+s2​1​=a1​​,s1​s2​=aL.

The reciprocal sum follows by replacing s2s_2s2​ with a(1+t2)/t2a(1+t^2)/t^2a(1+t2)/t2. Use it when a question gives focal distances rather than endpoint coordinates. A genuine finite focal chord has s1,s2>as_1,s_2>as1​,s2​>a.

If the chord makes angle θ\thetaθ with the axis, with sin⁡θ≠0\sin\theta\ne0sinθ=0,

L=4asin⁡2θ.\boxed{L=\frac{4a}{\sin^2\theta}}.L=sin2θ4a​​.

Why? Its slope is 2/(t−1/t)2/(t-1/t)2/(t−1/t), so 4cot⁡2θ=(t−1/t)24\cot^2\theta=(t-1/t)^24cot2θ=(t−1/t)2. Then L=a[(t−1/t)2+4]=4a(1+cot⁡2θ)L=a[(t-1/t)^2+4]=4a(1+\cot^2\theta)L=a[(t−1/t)2+4]=4a(1+cot2θ).

Important for JEE Main: a focal chord is at least 4a4a4a long. The minimum occurs at θ=90∘\theta=90^\circθ=90∘, the latus rectum. The excluded axis direction sin⁡θ=0\sin\theta=0sinθ=0 has no finite second endpoint.

Concept C07 — Normal, subnormal and counting normals

A normal is the line through a curve point perpendicular to its tangent. At P(t)P(t)P(t), the tangent slope is 1/t1/t1/t when t≠0t\ne0t=0, so the normal slope is −t-t−t.

y−2at=−t(x−at2)⟹y=−tx+2at+at3.y-2at=-t(x-at^2) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{y=-tx+2at+at^3}.y−2at=−t(x−at2)⟹y=−tx+2at+at3​.

It includes the vertex case t=0t=0t=0, giving the horizontal axis y=0y=0y=0. If the normal slope itself is called m=−tm=-tm=−t, the form is

y=mx−2am−am3.\boxed{y=mx-2am-am^3}.y=mx−2am−am3​.

Do not interchange mmm and ttt without the minus sign.

For normals passing through (x0,y0)(x_0,y_0)(x0​,y0​), substitute that point:

at3+(2a−x0)t−y0=0.at^3+(2a-x_0)t-y_0=0.at3+(2a−x0​)t−y0​=0.

Each real root gives a normal. A cubic has at most three real roots. To count them in Q10, we show three separate intervals with sign changes. We do not need the long formula for cubic roots. A plotted crossing suggests the count; exact signs prove it.

Subnormal: from P=(x1,y1)P=(x_1,y_1)P=(x1​,y1​), drop a perpendicular to the axis at M=(x1,0)M=(x_1,0)M=(x1​,0). Let the normal meet the axis at NNN. The subnormal is the axis segment MNMNMN, not the sloping segment PNPNPN.

For a nonvertex point, the normal equation gives N=(x1+2a,0)N=(x_1+2a,0)N=(x1​+2a,0), so

MN=2a.\boxed{MN=2a}.MN=2a​.

If TTT is the tangent's axis intercept, T=(−x1,0)T=(-x_1,0)T=(−x1​,0), so the subtangent TM=2x1TM=2x_1TM=2x1​. Only the subnormal stays constant as the point moves. In Q22 they happen to be equal because x1=ax_1=ax1​=a.

The corresponding sloping lengths follow from the right triangles:

PN=y12+4a2,PT=y12+4x12.PN=\sqrt{y_1^2+4a^2},\qquad PT=\sqrt{y_1^2+4x_1^2}.PN=y12​+4a2​,PT=y12​+4x12​​.

These projected-intercept constructions assume a nonvertex point. At the vertex, the normal is the axis itself, so it does not have one uniquely defined axis-intersection point NNN.

Concept C08 — A chord midpoint need not be on the curve

Suppose the midpoint is M=(h,k)M=(h,k)M=(h,k) and endpoints are (h+u,k+v)(h+u,k+v)(h+u,k+v), (h−u,k−v)(h-u,k-v)(h−u,k−v). Both endpoints obey y2=4axy^2=4axy2=4ax:

(k+v)2=4a(h+u),(k−v)2=4a(h−u).(k+v)^2=4a(h+u),\qquad (k-v)^2=4a(h-u).(k+v)2=4a(h+u),(k−v)2=4a(h−u).

Subtract:

4kv=8au⟹kv=2au.4kv=8au\quad\Longrightarrow\quad kv=2au.4kv=8au⟹kv=2au.

So the line through the midpoint in direction (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) is

k(y−k)=2a(x−h).\boxed{k(y-k)=2a(x-h)}.k(y−k)=2a(x−h)​.

It also works for k=0k=0k=0, giving a vertical chord x=hx=hx=h. A nonzero real chord requires

4ah−k2>0.\boxed{4ah-k^2>0}.4ah−k2>0​.

Indeed, for endpoint parameters t1,t2t_1,t_2t1​,t2​, that difference equals a2(t1−t2)2a^2(t_1-t_2)^2a2(t1​−t2​)2. Zero is a collapsed chord, not two different endpoints.

Do not use the tangent-at-point formula at a midpoint without checking the curve equation. Q25's (2,1)(2,1)(2,1) has 1≠8(2)1\ne8(2)1=8(2), so it is not a valid tangent contact point.

Concept C09 — Feet from the focus lie on the vertex tangent

For P(t)P(t)P(t), write its tangent as x−ty+at2=0x-ty+at^2=0x−ty+at2=0, with normal (1,−t)(1,-t)(1,−t). From focus F=(a,0)F=(a,0)F=(a,0), the perpendicular-foot formula from Straight Lines gives

H=F−a+at21+t2(1,−t)=(a,0)−a(1,−t).H=F-\frac{a+at^2}{1+t^2}(1,-t) =(a,0)-a(1,-t).H=F−1+t2a+at2​(1,−t)=(a,0)−a(1,−t).

Thus

H=(0,at).\boxed{H=(0,at)}.H=(0,at)​.

As ttt runs over all real numbers, atatat runs over all real heights. The complete foot locus is therefore x=0x=0x=0, the vertex tangent.

Why parameter form matters: t=0t=0t=0 gives the vertex tangent x=0x=0x=0 and foot (0,0)(0,0)(0,0). Finite-slope form would miss that tangent unless checked separately.

For a shifted or rotated parabola, apply the same geometry: the feet lie on its own vertex tangent, not automatically on the original coordinate yyy-axis.

Concept C10 — Distances: remove what you can using the curve relation

For a point on y2=4axy^2=4axy2=4ax, x≥0x\ge0x≥0. Use this equation before expanding many unknowns.

To a line: the point P(t)=(at2,2at)P(t)=(at^2,2at)P(t)=(at2,2at) has distance from Ax+By+C=0Ax+By+C=0Ax+By+C=0

d(t)=∣Aat2+2aBt+C∣A2+B2.\boxed{d(t)=\frac{|Aat^2+2aBt+C|}{\sqrt{A^2+B^2}}}.d(t)=A2+B2​∣Aat2+2aBt+C∣​​.

First check whether the numerator can be zero: an intersection would give minimum distance zero. If it never vanishes, determine its sign, complete the square and minimize its absolute value. Do not drop the modulus before checking the sign.

To an axis point (p,0)(p,0)(p,0): replace y2y^2y2 directly:

D2=(x−p)2+y2=(x−p)2+4ax=[x−(p−2a)]2+4a(p−a),x≥0.\begin{aligned} D^2&=(x-p)^2+y^2\\ &=(x-p)^2+4ax\\ &=[x-(p-2a)]^2+4a(p-a),\qquad x\ge0. \end{aligned}D2​=(x−p)2+y2=(x−p)2+4ax=[x−(p−2a)]2+4a(p−a),x≥0.​

If p>2ap>2ap>2a, equality is possible at x=p−2a>0x=p-2a>0x=p−2a>0, giving two symmetric nearest points and Dmin⁡2=4a(p−a)D_{\min}^2=4a(p-a)Dmin2​=4a(p−a). If p≤2ap\le2ap≤2a, the allowed minimum is at the vertex x=0x=0x=0, giving Dmin⁡2=p2D_{\min}^2=p^2Dmin2​=p2. At equality p=2ap=2ap=2a, the two candidate points merge into that one vertex.

Important for JEE Main: minimizing D2D^2D2 is equivalent to minimizing the nonnegative distance DDD, and avoids a square root. Respect x≥0x\ge0x≥0, and read whether the final question asks for DDD or D2D^2D2.

Concept C11 — A locus needs the original distances and a reverse check

For focus F=(h,k)F=(h,k)F=(h,k) and directrix Ax+By+C=0Ax+By+C=0Ax+By+C=0, with A2+B2>0A^2+B^2>0A2+B2>0 and focus off the line, write

(x−h)2+(y−k)2=∣Ax+By+C∣A2+B2.\boxed{\sqrt{(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2} =\frac{|Ax+By+C|}{\sqrt{A^2+B^2}}}.(x−h)2+(y−k)2​=A2+B2​∣Ax+By+C∣​​.

Both sides are nonnegative, so squaring preserves the equality. The denominator is essential: the raw line expression is not yet a distance.

A sloping directrix usually produces a rotated parabola. You can derive its equation without learning a full rotation-formula method. A graph must use the actual rotated geometry, not an axis-aligned substitute.

Midpoints from a fixed vertex: if the vertex is (0,0)(0,0)(0,0) and M=(x,y)M=(x,y)M=(x,y), the other endpoint is (2x,2y)(2x,2y)(2x,2y). Substitute that endpoint into the original parabola. Remove the vertex from the midpoint locus when a nonzero chord is required.

Always check the reverse: can each retained locus point reconstruct a valid original endpoint or distance equality?

Concept C12 — Area: identify upper/lower or right/left boundaries

For y2=4axy^2=4axy2=4ax, the upper branch is 2ax2\sqrt{ax}2ax​ and lower branch is −2ax-2\sqrt{ax}−2ax​.

With a closing vertical line x=b>0x=b>0x=b>0,

A=∫0b[2ax−(−2ax)]dx=∫0b4ax dx=83a b3/2.\begin{aligned} A&=\int_0^b\left[2\sqrt{ax}-(-2\sqrt{ax})\right]dx\\ &=\int_0^b4\sqrt{ax}\,dx =\boxed{\frac83\sqrt a\,b^{3/2}}. \end{aligned}A​=∫0b​[2ax​−(−2ax​)]dx=∫0b​4ax​dx=38​a​b3/2​.​

Alternatively, horizontal strips use right x=bx=bx=b minus left x=y2/(4a)x=y^2/(4a)x=y2/(4a), with −2ab≤y≤2ab-2\sqrt{ab}\le y\le2\sqrt{ab}−2ab​≤y≤2ab​.

For the line y=mxy=mxy=mx, m≠0m\ne0m=0, meeting the vertex, the other intersection has x=4a/m2x=4a/m^2x=4a/m2, y=4a/my=4a/my=4a/m. The enclosed area is 8a2/(3∣m∣3)8a^2/(3|m|^3)8a2/(3∣m∣3). Rebuild it from strip widths if the formula is not familiar; Q20 shows both orientations for a=m=1a=m=1a=m=1.

Two checks: an ordinary area cannot be negative, and the endpoints must satisfy both boundary equations. A single branch or an arbitrary integration limit does not describe the requested region.

Concept C13 — A useful connection: why a parabola focuses parallel rays

This is a geometric connection to reflection, not an extra formula you must learn for the supplied numerical questions.

From C09, the focus's foot on the tangent at P(t)P(t)P(t) is H=(0,at)H=(0,at)H=(0,at). Reflect the focus F=(a,0)F=(a,0)F=(a,0) across that tangent:

F′=2H−F=(−a,2at).F'=2H-F=(-a,2at).F′=2H−F=(−a,2at).

This point lies on the directrix. It also has the same height as P(t)=(at2,2at)P(t)=(at^2,2at)P(t)=(at2,2at), so PF′PF'PF′ is parallel to the axis.

A mirror line makes equal angles with a segment and its reflection. Thus the tangent gives equal incidence/reflection angles between an incoming axis-parallel ray and the outgoing ray towards the focus. A ray sent from the focus reflects parallel to the axis in the reverse direction.

This joins three ideas already taught: equal focus/directrix distances, the foot-of-perpendicular locus, and reflection in a straight line. The picture uses the actual example y2=4xy^2=4xy2=4x, P=(4,4)P=(4,4)P=(4,4), F=(1,0)F=(1,0)F=(1,0), H=(0,2)H=(0,2)H=(0,2) and F′=(−1,4)F'=(-1,4)F′=(−1,4).

Method habit: identify the orientation, define the point, and write the condition that actually matches the question. A tangent point, normal point, chord midpoint and focus are different objects. Use one clear main route, then read the alternative view to strengthen the connection.

Worked solutions to the 30 PDF questions

Read the question first. Notice the pattern, choose a route, then calculate. Alternative methods below are fully visible.

Question 1 — The unsquared variable and its sign decide the opening

PDF page 92 | MCQ | Notes: C01,C02

The focus of the parabola x2=−8yx^2=-8yx2=−8y is

  • (a) (0,2)(0,2)(0,2)
  • (b) (−2,0)(-2,0)(−2,0)
  • (c) (2,0)(2,0)(2,0)
  • (d) (0,−2)(0,-2)(0,−2)

First read the direction. In x2=−8yx^2=-8yx2=−8y, xxx is squared and yyy is unsquared. The axis is vertical. The minus sign makes the opening downward.

Compare with x2=−4ayx^2=-4ayx2=−4ay, where a>0a>0a>0:

4a=8⟹a=2.4a=8\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a=2.4a=8⟹a=2.

The vertex is (0,0)(0,0)(0,0), and the focus is aaa units below it:

F=(0,−2);(d).\boxed{F=(0,-2);\quad\text{(d)}}.F=(0,−2);(d)​.

Check with the definition: its directrix is y=2y=2y=2. The point (4,−2)(4,-2)(4,−2) obeys 16=−8(−2)16=-8(-2)16=−8(−2); its focus distance is 4, and its perpendicular distance to y=2y=2y=2 is also 4. A focus on the xxx-axis would not match this vertical opening.

Question 2 — The focus lies along the axis from the vertex

PDF page 92 | MCQ | Notes: C02

A parabola has vertex (1,2)(1,2)(1,2) and focus (3,2)(3,2)(3,2). Its equation is

  • (a) (y−2)2=4(x−1)(y-2)^2=4(x-1)(y−2)2=4(x−1)
  • (b) (y−2)2=8(x−1)(y-2)^2=8(x-1)(y−2)2=8(x−1)
  • (c) (x−1)2=8(y−2)(x-1)^2=8(y-2)(x−1)2=8(y−2)
  • (d) (y−2)2=8(x+1)(y-2)^2=8(x+1)(y−2)2=8(x+1)

The vertex and focus tell the axis before the equation. Both have height 2, so the axis is horizontal, y=2y=2y=2. The focus is to the right of the vertex, so the parabola opens right.

a=VF=3−1=2.a=VF=3-1=2.a=VF=3−1=2.

Use the shifted right-opening form:

(y−k)2=4a(x−h).(y-k)^2=4a(x-h).(y−k)2=4a(x−h).

With (h,k)=(1,2)(h,k)=(1,2)(h,k)=(1,2) and a=2a=2a=2,

(y−2)2=8(x−1);(b).\boxed{(y-2)^2=8(x-1);\quad\text{(b)}}.(y−2)2=8(x−1);(b)​.

Check: its directrix is x=1−2=−1x=1-2=-1x=1−2=−1. The vertex (1,2)(1,2)(1,2) is 2 units from both focus (3,2)(3,2)(3,2) and that directrix. The focus lies in the opening direction.

Fast option insight: an equation with (x−1)2(x-1)^2(x−1)2 would have a vertical axis, so option (c) fails the axis test before any arithmetic.

Question 3 — Complete the square before reading the latus rectum

PDF page 92 | MCQ | Notes: C02,C03

The length of the latus rectum of the parabola x2+6x−12y+33=0x^2+6x-12y+33=0x2+6x−12y+33=0 is

  • (a) 121212
  • (b) 666
  • (c) 333
  • (d) 242424

Do not read 4a4a4a until the square is complete.

x2+6x−12y+33=0⟹(x+3)2=12y−24=12(y−2).x^2+6x-12y+33=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (x+3)^2=12y-24=12(y-2).x2+6x−12y+33=0⟹(x+3)2=12y−24=12(y−2).

This opens up from vertex (−3,2)(-3,2)(−3,2). Comparing with (x−h)2=4a(y−k)(x-h)^2=4a(y-k)(x−h)2=4a(y−k) gives 4a=124a=124a=12, a=3a=3a=3.

The latus rectum is the focal chord perpendicular to the axis, so its length is

4a=12;(a).\boxed{4a=12;\quad\text{(a)}}.4a=12;(a)​.

Coordinate check: the focus is (−3,5)(-3,5)(−3,5). Put y=5y=5y=5 in the completed equation: (x+3)2=36(x+3)^2=36(x+3)2=36, giving endpoints (−9,5),(3,5)(-9,5),(3,5)(−9,5),(3,5). Their horizontal separation is 3−(−9)=123-(-9)=123−(−9)=12. The focal length 3 is not the requested chord length.

Question 4 — The given point is on the parabola, so use a tangent there

PDF page 92 | MCQ | Notes: C05

The equation of the tangent to the parabola y2=8xy^2=8xy2=8x at the point (2,4)(2,4)(2,4) is

  • (a) x+y−6=0x+y-6=0x+y−6=0
  • (b) 2x−y=02x-y=02x−y=0
  • (c) x−y+2=0x-y+2=0x−y+2=0
  • (d) x−2y+6=0x-2y+6=0x−2y+6=0

First check that the supplied point is on the curve: 42=8(2)=164^2=8(2)=1642=8(2)=16. Good, the tangent-at-point formula applies.

For y2=4axy^2=4axy2=4ax, here a=2a=2a=2:

yy1=2a(x+x1)⟹4y=4(x+2).yy_1=2a(x+x_1) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 4y=4(x+2).yy1​=2a(x+x1​)⟹4y=4(x+2).

Therefore

x−y+2=0;(c).\boxed{x-y+2=0;\quad\text{(c)}}.x−y+2=0;(c)​.

Another possible approach — the derivative: 2yy′=82yy'=82yy′=8, so y′=4/y=1y'=4/y=1y′=4/y=1 at (2,4)(2,4)(2,4). Then y−4=x−2y-4=x-2y−4=x−2 gives the same line.

Check tangency: substituting y=x+2y=x+2y=x+2 into y2=8xy^2=8xy2=8x gives (x+2)2=8x(x+2)^2=8x(x+2)2=8x, or (x−2)2=0(x-2)^2=0(x−2)2=0. The repeated contact is precisely the given point.

Question 5 — A repeated intersection is the tangency condition

PDF page 92 | Numerical value | Notes: C05

If the line x−2y+c=0x-2y+c=0x−2y+c=0 touches the parabola y2=8xy^2=8xy2=8x, then c=c=c= ____.

The line's slope is fixed; its intercept is unknown. Rearrange:

y=12x+c2.y=\frac12x+\frac c2.y=21​x+2c​.

For y2=4axy^2=4axy2=4ax with a=2a=2a=2, a finite-slope tangent is y=mx+a/my=mx+a/my=mx+a/m. At m=1/2m=1/2m=1/2, its intercept must be

am=21/2=4.\frac am=\frac2{1/2}=4.ma​=1/22​=4.

Thus c/2=4c/2=4c/2=4, giving

c=8.\boxed{c=8}.c=8​.

Another possible approach — repeated intersection: substitute x=2y−cx=2y-cx=2y−c into the parabola:

y2=16y−8c⟹y2−16y+8c=0.y^2=16y-8c \quad\Longrightarrow\quad y^2-16y+8c=0.y2=16y−8c⟹y2−16y+8c=0.

Tangency requires discriminant zero: 256−32c=0256-32c=0256−32c=0, so c=8c=8c=8. Then the root is y=8y=8y=8, x=8x=8x=8, checking the actual contact point.

Fast coefficient check: for Ax+By+C=0Ax+By+C=0Ax+By+C=0, the tangent condition is AC=aB2AC=aB^2AC=aB2. Here c=2(−2)2=8c=2(-2)^2=8c=2(−2)2=8.

Question 6 — A focal chord must pass through the focus

PDF page 92 | Numerical value | Notes: C04,C06

One end of a focal chord of y2=8xy^2=8xy2=8x is (8,8)(8,8)(8,8). The length of this focal chord is ____.

A focal chord passes through the focus. Here 4a=84a=84a=8, so a=2a=2a=2 and F=(2,0)F=(2,0)F=(2,0).

The given endpoint P=(8,8)P=(8,8)P=(8,8) has 2at=82at=82at=8, hence t=2t=2t=2. Its partner parameter must satisfy tt2=−1tt_2=-1tt2​=−1, giving t2=−1/2t_2=-1/2t2​=−1/2.

Q=(at22,2at2)=(12,−2).Q=(at_2^2,2at_2)=\left(\frac12,-2\right).Q=(at22​,2at2​)=(21​,−2).

The full length is

PQ=(8−12)2+(8+2)2=2254+100=252=12.5.PQ=\sqrt{\left(8-\frac12\right)^2+(8+2)^2} =\sqrt{\frac{225}{4}+100} =\boxed{\frac{25}{2}=12.5}.PQ=(8−21​)2+(8+2)2​=4225​+100​=225​=12.5​.

Another shorter approach — add focal distances: the focus lies between the two ends, so

PQ=PF+FQ=(8+2)+(12+2)=10+52=252.PQ=PF+FQ=(8+2)+\left(\frac12+2\right)=10+\frac52=\frac{25}{2}.PQ=PF+FQ=(8+2)+(21​+2)=10+25​=225​.

A third useful check: L=a(t+1/t)2=2(2+1/2)2=25/2L=a(t+1/t)^2=2(2+1/2)^2=25/2L=a(t+1/t)2=2(2+1/2)2=25/2. These agree because the focal-chord parameter identity and focal-distance definition describe the same geometry.

Question 7 — A line through the focus can be the axis itself

PDF page 92 | MCQ | Notes: C01,C03

Statement I: Every line passing through the focus of a parabola meets the parabola in exactly two points.

Statement II: The axis of a parabola meets the parabola at exactly one point.

Choose the correct option.

  • (a) Statement I is false but Statement II is true
  • (b) Both Statement I and Statement II are true
  • (c) Both Statement I and Statement II are false
  • (d) Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Look for an exception to “every line.” The axis itself passes through the focus. On the representative parabola y2=4axy^2=4axy2=4ax, the axis is y=0y=0y=0:

0=4ax⟹x=0.0=4ax\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=0.0=4ax⟹x=0.

It meets the parabola only at the vertex.

So Statement I is false. This same fact makes Statement II true.

I false, II true;(a).\boxed{\text{I false, II true;\quad (a)}}.I false, II true;(a)​.

The useful distinction: passing through the focus does not automatically create two finite endpoints. A focal chord requires those two distinct endpoints. Also, a single intersection with an unbounded curve does not automatically mean the line is tangent: the axis here is the vertex's normal, while its tangent is perpendicular to the axis.

Question 9 — A normal is perpendicular to the tangent at the same point

PDF page 93 | MCQ | Notes: C07

The equation of the normal to y2=4xy^2=4xy2=4x at the point (1,2)(1,2)(1,2) is

  • (a) x−y=−1x-y=-1x−y=−1
  • (b) x+y=1x+y=1x+y=1
  • (c) 2x+y=42x+y=42x+y=4
  • (d) x+y=3x+y=3x+y=3

A normal is perpendicular to the tangent at the same point. Differentiate the curve:

2yy′=4,y′=2y.2yy'=4,\qquad y'=\frac2y.2yy′=4,y′=y2​.

At P=(1,2)P=(1,2)P=(1,2) the tangent slope is 1, so the normal slope is −1-1−1.

Through (1,2)(1,2)(1,2),

y−2=−(x−1)⟹x+y=3;(d).y-2=-(x-1) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{x+y=3;\quad\text{(d)}}.y−2=−(x−1)⟹x+y=3;(d)​.

Check: (1,2)(1,2)(1,2) lies on both the parabola and normal, and tangent slope times normal slope is 1(−1)=−11(-1)=-11(−1)=−1.

Another possible approach: P=(at2,2at)P=(at^2,2at)P=(at2,2at) with a=1a=1a=1 gives t=1t=1t=1. The parameter normal y=−tx+2at+at3y=-tx+2at+at^3y=−tx+2at+at3 becomes y=−x+3y=-x+3y=−x+3. This is a quick exam form after its meaning is understood.

Question 10 — Count real normal slopes without solving the cubic explicitly

PDF page 93 | MCQ | Notes: C07

The number of distinct normals that can be drawn to the parabola y2=4xy^2=4xy2=4x from the point (5,1)(5,1)(5,1) is

  • (a) 111
  • (b) 333
  • (c) 222
  • (d) 000

We need a count, not the exact three slopes. Let mmm be a normal's slope, not the tangent parameter. For a=1a=1a=1, the normal family is

y=mx−2m−m3.y=mx-2m-m^3.y=mx−2m−m3.

Passing through (5,1)(5,1)(5,1) gives

1=5m−2m−m3⟹f(m)=m3−3m+1=0.1=5m-2m-m^3 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(m)=m^3-3m+1=0.1=5m−2m−m3⟹f(m)=m3−3m+1=0.

Trying the general cubic-root formula would create unnecessary calculation. Instead, find separate intervals containing roots:

m−2−1012f(m)−131−13\begin{array}{c|rrrrr} m&-2&-1&0&1&2\\\hline f(m)&-1&3&1&-1&3 \end{array}mf(m)​−2−1​−13​01​1−1​23​​

The continuous polynomial changes sign on three disjoint intervals:

(−2,−1),(0,1),(1,2).(-2,-1),\qquad(0,1),\qquad(1,2).(−2,−1),(0,1),(1,2).

Each interval contains a real root. A cubic has at most three roots, so there are exactly three distinct slopes. Each different slope through the same point gives a different normal:

3;(b).\boxed{3;\quad\text{(b)}}.3;(b)​.

Check that the family covers the possibilities: every finite point on this right-opening parabola has normal slope −t-t−t, including slope 0 at the vertex. There is no omitted vertical normal.

Another root-count view: f′(m)=3(m2−1)f'(m)=3(m^2-1)f′(m)=3(m2−1) gives turning inputs −1,1-1,1−1,1, where the values are 3 and −1-1−1. With the cubic tending to opposite infinities at the two ends, this also gives three crossings. The sign-interval route needs fewer prerequisites.

Question 11 — Focal distance equals distance to the directrix

PDF page 93 | Numerical value | Notes: C03

A point on the parabola y2=16xy^2=16xy2=16x is at a distance 101010 from the focus. The square of its ordinate is ____.

The focus–directrix definition saves a square root. Since y2=16xy^2=16xy2=16x, a=4a=4a=4, the focus is (4,0)(4,0)(4,0) and the directrix is x=−4x=-4x=−4.

For any curve point, x≥0x\ge0x≥0, so its perpendicular distance to the directrix is x+4x+4x+4. This equals its focal distance.

Thus

x+4=10⟹x=6.x+4=10\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=6.x+4=10⟹x=6.

Now the parabola equation gives

y2=16(6)=96.\boxed{y^2=16(6)=96}.y2=16(6)=96​.

Both ordinates work: y=±96y=\pm\sqrt{96}y=±96​, and the question asks for their common square.

Coordinate check: its line passes through focus (4,0)(4,0)(4,0) and is x=4x=4x=4. Substitution gives y2=64y^2=64y2=64, so its endpoints are (4,8),(4,−8)(4,8),(4,-8)(4,8),(4,−8). Their separation is 16.

Do not infer opening direction from the negative ordinate: upper and lower points belong to the same right-opening parabola. The sign of the unsquared xxx coefficient, not the chosen point's yyy sign, decides the opening.

Question 25 — A chord midpoint need not lie on the parabola

PDF page 94 | MCQ | Notes: C08

The equation of the chord of the parabola y2=8xy^2=8xy2=8x whose midpoint is (2,1)(2,1)(2,1) is

  • (a) 4x+y−9=04x+y-9=04x+y−9=0
  • (b) x−4y+2=0x-4y+2=0x−4y+2=0
  • (c) 4x−y−1=04x-y-1=04x−y−1=0
  • (d) 4x−y−7=04x-y-7=04x−y−7=0

Do not use a tangent formula at the midpoint. The point (2,1)(2,1)(2,1) is not on y2=8xy^2=8xy2=8x, since 1≠161\ne161=16. We need a chord with two endpoints placed equally around it.

Write the endpoints as

A=(2+u,1+v),B=(2−u,1−v).A=(2+u,1+v),\qquad B=(2-u,1-v).A=(2+u,1+v),B=(2−u,1−v).

Both lie on the curve:

(1+v)2=8(2+u),(1−v)2=8(2−u).(1+v)^2=8(2+u),\qquad (1-v)^2=8(2-u).(1+v)2=8(2+u),(1−v)2=8(2−u).

Subtract to remove the matching squares:

4v=16u⟹v=4u.4v=16u\quad\Longrightarrow\quad v=4u.4v=16u⟹v=4u.

Thus the chord direction has slope 4 and passes through (2,1)(2,1)(2,1):

y−1=4(x−2)⟹4x−y−7=0;(d).y-1=4(x-2) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{4x-y-7=0;\quad\text{(d)}}.y−1=4(x−2)⟹4x−y−7=0;(d)​.

Fast exam version: the midpoint-chord formula is k(y−k)=2a(x−h)k(y-k)=2a(x-h)k(y−k)=2a(x−h). With a=2,h=2,k=1a=2,h=2,k=1a=2,h=2,k=1, it gives the same line directly.

Independent endpoint check: substituting y=4x−7y=4x-7y=4x−7 gives endpoints

(2±154, 1±15).\left(2\pm\frac{\sqrt{15}}4,\ 1\pm\sqrt{15}\right).(2±415​​, 1±15​).

Both satisfy the parabola and their midpoint is (2,1)(2,1)(2,1). Their existence also agrees with 4ah−k2=16−1=15>04ah-k^2=16-1=15>04ah−k2=16−1=15>0.

Question 26 — Square the distance and keep both symmetric minimizing points

PDF page 94 | Numerical value | Notes: C10

The square of the minimum distance of the point (6,0)(6,0)(6,0) from the parabola y2=4xy^2=4xy2=4x is ____.

The question asks for distance squared, so avoid an unnecessary square root. For any curve point (x,y)(x,y)(x,y),

D2=(x−6)2+y2.D^2=(x-6)^2+y^2.D2=(x−6)2+y2.

The parabola gives y2=4xy^2=4xy2=4x and x≥0x\ge0x≥0. Substitute before differentiating:

D2=(x−6)2+4x=x2−8x+36=(x−4)2+20.D^2=(x-6)^2+4x=x^2-8x+36=(x-4)^2+20.D2=(x−6)2+4x=x2−8x+36=(x−4)2+20.

The square is at least zero, and x=4x=4x=4 is allowed. Hence

Dmin⁡2=20.\boxed{D_{\min}^2=20}.Dmin2​=20​.

Keep both points: at x=4x=4x=4, y=±4y=\pm4y=±4. Each gives D2=(4−6)2+16=20D^2=(4-6)^2+16=20D2=(4−6)2+16=20. There is no unique nearest point.

Another possible approach — parameter and derivative: with (x,y)=(t2,2t)(x,y)=(t^2,2t)(x,y)=(t2,2t),

D2=t4−8t2+36,ddtD2=4t(t2−4).D^2=t^4-8t^2+36,\qquad \frac d{dt}D^2=4t(t^2-4).D2=t4−8t2+36,dtd​D2=4t(t2−4).

Candidates are t=0,±2t=0,\pm2t=0,±2, with values 36, 20, 20. Since D2→∞D^2\to\inftyD2→∞ as ∣t∣→∞|t|\to\infty∣t∣→∞, the smallest is 20. Completing the square is shorter and proves the global lower bound immediately.

Geometric check: each shortest segment is normal to the parabola at its endpoint, as the small right-angle marks show.

Question 27 — This parabola opens upward, so use the vertical form

PDF page 94 | MCQ | Notes: C02,C05

The tangent to the parabola x2=4yx^2=4yx2=4y at the point (4,4)(4,4)(4,4) is

  • (a) 2x−y−4=02x-y-4=02x−y−4=0
  • (b) 2x+y−12=02x+y-12=02x+y−12=0
  • (c) x−2y+4=0x-2y+4=0x−2y+4=0
  • (d) x−y=0x-y=0x−y=0

Notice the orientation: x2=4yx^2=4yx2=4y opens upward. The tangent formula must match this form.

Differentiate:

2x=4y′⟹y′=x2.2x=4y'\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y'=\frac x2.2x=4y′⟹y′=2x​.

At (4,4)(4,4)(4,4), slope is 2. Therefore

y−4=2(x−4)⟹2x−y−4=0;(a).y-4=2(x-4) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{2x-y-4=0;\quad\text{(a)}}.y−4=2(x−4)⟹2x−y−4=0;(a)​.

Fast formula view: for x2=4ayx^2=4ayx2=4ay, the tangent is xx1=2a(y+y1)xx_1=2a(y+y_1)xx1​=2a(y+y1​). Here it gives 4x=2(y+4)4x=2(y+4)4x=2(y+4), the same equation.

Check: substitute y=2x−4y=2x-4y=2x−4 into the original curve:

x2=4(2x−4)⟹(x−4)2=0.x^2=4(2x-4)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(x-4)^2=0.x2=4(2x−4)⟹(x−4)2=0.

Why copying the sideways formula fails: yy1=2a(x+x1)yy_1=2a(x+x_1)yy1​=2a(x+x1​) belongs to y2=4axy^2=4axy2=4ax, not this upward form. The derivative route automatically respects which variable is squared.

Question 28 — The tangent-slope quadratic tells how many real tangents exist

PDF page 95 | MCQ | Notes: C05

The number of tangents that can be drawn from the point (1,3)(1,3)(1,3) to the parabola y2=4xy^2=4xy2=4x is

  • (a) 000
  • (b) 111
  • (c) 222
  • (d) 333

Count real tangent contacts rather than guessing from a sketch. The tangent at parameter ttt to y2=4xy^2=4xy2=4x is ty=x+t2ty=x+t^2ty=x+t2.

For it to pass through (1,3)(1,3)(1,3),

3t=1+t2⟹t2−3t+1=0.3t=1+t^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad t^2-3t+1=0.3t=1+t2⟹t2−3t+1=0.

Its discriminant is 9−4=5>09-4=5>09−4=5>0, so there are two distinct real parameters, hence two distinct tangent lines:

2;(c).\boxed{2;\quad\text{(c)}}.2;(c)​.

Check: the parameters are (3±5)/2(3\pm\sqrt5)/2(3±5​)/2, both real. Neither is zero, so neither line is the vertical vertex tangent. The source point has y2−4x=9−4=5>0y^2-4x=9-4=5>0y2−4x=9−4=5>0, agreeing with the two-tangent criterion.

The graph helps visualize the two contacts, but the positive discriminant establishes their exact count.

Question 29 — The coefficient of x squared is not the focal length

PDF page 95 | MCQ | Notes: C02

The focus of the parabola y=2x2−4x+3y=2x^2-4x+3y=2x2−4x+3 is

Complete the square and compare with the standard form.

y=2x2−4x+3=2(x−1)2+1.y=2x^2-4x+3 =2(x-1)^2+1.y=2x2−4x+3=2(x−1)2+1.

So the vertex is (1,1)(1,1)(1,1), and

(x−1)2=12(y−1)=4a(y−1).(x-1)^2=\frac12(y-1)=4a(y-1).(x−1)2=21​(y−1)=4a(y−1).

Thus 4a=1/24a=1/24a=1/2 and a=1/8a=1/8a=1/8, not 2.

The parabola opens up, so move 1/81/81/8 above the vertex:

F=(1,1+18)=(1,98);(a).\boxed{F=\left(1,1+\frac18\right)=\left(1,\frac98\right);\quad\text{(a)}}.F=(1,1+81​)=(1,89​);(a)​.

Why the diagram is zoomed: the focus is only 0.1250.1250.125 units above the vertex. The frame labels show original coordinates; its edges are not the coordinate-origin axes.

matching its directrix distance 3/2−7/8=5/83/2-7/8=5/83/2−7/8=5/8.

Question 30 — A circle on a diameter uses half that diameter as its radius

PDF page 95 | MCQ | Notes: C03

The equation of the circle described on the latus rectum of the parabola y2=8xy^2=8xy2=8x as diameter is

  • (a) x2+y2−4x+4=0x^2+y^2-4x+4=0x2+y2−4x+4=0
  • (b) x2+y2−4x−4=0x^2+y^2-4x-4=0x2+y2−4x−4=0
  • (c) x2+y2−4x−12=0x^2+y^2-4x-12=0x2+y2−4x−12=0
  • (d) x2+y2+4x−12=0x^2+y^2+4x-12=0x2+y2+4x−12=0

Find the diameter that the question actually names. For y2=8xy^2=8xy2=8x, a=2a=2a=2. Its latus rectum lies on x=2x=2x=2 and has endpoints

A=(2,4),B=(2,−4).A=(2,4),\qquad B=(2,-4).A=(2,4),B=(2,−4).

Their midpoint is (2,0)(2,0)(2,0) and their separation is 8. Hence the required circle has centre (2,0)(2,0)(2,0) and radius 4:

(x−2)2+y2=16⟹x2+y2−4x−12=0;(c).(x-2)^2+y^2=16 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{x^2+y^2-4x-12=0;\quad\text{(c)}}.(x−2)2+y2=16⟹x2+y2−4x−12=0;(c)​.

Another possible approach — diameter formula from Circles:

(x−2)(x−2)+(y−4)(y+4)=0.(x-2)(x-2)+(y-4)(y+4)=0.(x−2)(x−2)+(y−4)(y+4)=0.

It expands into the same equation.

Check the three different lengths: focal length a=2a=2a=2, latus-rectum diameter 4a=84a=84a=8, circle radius 2a=42a=42a=4. Using the focal length as the circle radius would answer a different construction.

After this chapter

Start with the focus, directrix, vertex and opening. Then decide whether the moving object is a curve point, tangent contact, normal contact or chord midpoint. Keep those roles separate. Use exact algebra to support the picture, check the original conditions and retain all valid symmetric points. All alternative views above are plain visible content for the later booklet.
